fetched_contents.text: Does soil burn severity affect the post-fire runoff and interrill erosion response? A review based on meta-analysis of field rainfall simulation data Introduction Wildfire has been a natural disturbance factor in most forest ecosystems since late Devonian times (Schmidt and Noack, 2000). However, mankind’s key role in present-day fire regimes, especially through changes in land cover/use, has turned wildfires into an environmental problem in various countries over the last five decades (Cerdà and Mataix-Solera, 2009). Amongst other environmental impacts, wildfire is widely regarded as the principal agent of soil erosion and land degradation in woodlands and shrublands (DeBano et al., 2005, Shakesby and Doerr, 2006, Shakesby, 2011). Fire-enhanced runoff and erosion are commonly attributed to the (partial or total) removal of the protective soil cover by vegetation and litter, in combination with heating-induced changes in soil properties such as aggregate stability and water repellency (Neary et al., 1999, Mataix-Solera and Guerrero, 2007, Ubeda and Outeiro, 2009, Varela et al., 2010). These changes can markedly enhance runoff and associated transport processes during the so-called window of disturbance, both at the hillslope and catchment scale (Prosser and Williams, 1998, Shakesby and Doerr, 2006, Shakesby, 2011, Prats et al., 2013). Soil burn severity is a commonly-used term to describe the heating-induced alterations to soil properties caused by fire. However, there is not a single and unique definition of this term (Keeley, 2009). Besides as an indicator of the direct impacts of fire on soil properties, soil burn severity is often used as an indicator of the fire’s indirect impacts on the hydrological and erosion response of recently burnt areas. Most of the soil burn indices that have been proposed are based on the amount of surface litter layer consumed, the visually-observable changes of the mineral soil surface, the amount and colour of the deposited ashes, and/or the amount of charcoal present after the combustion of the aboveground biomass (Ryan and Noste, 1985, Neary et al., 2005, Shakesby and Doerr, 2006, Jain et al., 2012, Vega et al., 2013a). An indicator that is more closely linked to the soil heating regime itself is that of the maximum soil temperatures reached (MTR) estimated from Near Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy of laboratory-heated and field soil samples (Arcenegui et al., 2008, Guerrero et al., 2007, Maia et al., 2012). The use of distinct burn-severity classifications will hamper a direct comparison of the results obtained by different studies. Wildfires often produce mosaics of areas with different soil burn severities (Robichaud et al., 2000, Maia et al., 2012, Vega et al., 2013a). These spatial patterns in burn severity are often important in identifying areas with a high risk of post-fire erosion (Benavides-Solorio and MacDonald, 2005, Mayor et al., 2007, Gimeno-Garcia et al., 2007, Chafer, 2008). In fact, mapping of soil burn severity has become an integral part of operational procedures in the USA to assess the risks of soil erosion and off-site impacts on downstream “values-at-risk” and, thereby, to prioritize emergency measures for reducing these risks (e.g., USDA, 1995, Parsons et al., 2010, Vega et al., 2013b). In the USA, a high soil burn severity is often associated with a decrease in ground cover, an increase in soil water repellency, and a decrease in infiltration (DeBano et al., 1998, Robichaud, 2000, Benavides-Solorio and MacDonald, 2001, Pierson et al., 2001, Robichaud et al., 2007). Even so, in other parts of the world the relationship between soil burn severity and post-fire erosion has not been extensively studied and remains to be fully quantified (Shakesby, 2011). The reviews on wildfire effects in the Mediterranean Basin by Pausas et al. (2008) and Shakesby (2011) did not include a comprehensive analysis of the role of burn severity. To gain further insight in this relationship between burn severity and post-fire erosion, the present study aimed to compile the existing rainfall simulation data from field studies across the world and to analyse them quantitatively by means of meta-analysis. Field rainfall simulations experiments (RSE’s) have been widely used to study the effects of fire on runoff and sediment losses (e.g., Emmerich and Cox, 1992, Robichaud, 2000, De Luis et al., 2003, Ferreira et al., 2005, Fernández et al., 2008, Groen and Woods, 2008). Nevertheless, the most comprehensive recent reviews on post-fire erosion (Shakesby and Doerr, 2006, Shakesby, 2011, Moody et al., 2013) have not included these RSE studies. The last review that did include them was that of Rulli et al. (2006). While the limitations of RSE’s as a research tool are well-established, RSE’s do permit a direct comparison of the hydrological and inter-rill erosion response of different study sites, distinct soil conservation measures and different times-since-fire (e.g., Cerdà, 1998, Nunes et al., 2009, Johansen et al., 2001a, Malvar et al., 2011, Fernández et al., 2012). Branch on biomass reduction’s direct effects on post-fire hydrology

Aboveground biomass reduction after wildfires primarily alters hydrology by removing the vegetation and litter that control interception and surface retention. The evidence here shows that fire removal of plants and litter reduces rainfall interception and surface water storage, which promotes rapid runoff and decreases ground-surface protection against raindrop impact and soil detachment [N2-R2]. Another source similarly states that reductions in ground cover abate surface retention of overland flow, allowing flow to concentrate and move downslope with greater erosive potential [N2-F1]. These mechanisms are central to why biomass loss increases direct runoff: the vegetation layer that would otherwise intercept some rainfall and store water on the surface is gone, leaving the land surface exposed to more immediate runoff generation [N2-R2][N2-F1].

Reduced surface roughness is another direct consequence of aboveground biomass loss. The same literature synthesis notes that reduced ground cover abates surface retention and allows overland flow to concentrate downslope [N2-F1]. This matters because surface roughness is a key factor in distributing runoff across a hillslope; when it is reduced, flow paths become more concentrated, flow velocity increases, and erosion potential rises. The evidence also links biomass loss to increased overland flow velocity and erosion, implying that the hydrologic response is not just more runoff but more energetic and more erosive flow [N2-R3][N2-F1].

The interaction with slope and vegetation structure is important because the effects of biomass reduction are amplified where slopes are steep. The USDA report explicitly says amplified runoff and erosion responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N4-F3]. In other words, biomass reduction interacts with topography: on gentle slopes, some surface retention and dispersion may still occur, but on steep slopes, even a moderate loss of cover can rapidly create conditions favorable to concentrated flow and high erosion rates [N4-F3]. This is consistent with the general idea that vegetation structure and slope together determine how rainfall is partitioned into infiltration, interception, and direct runoff [N2-F1][N4-F3].

Taken together, the direct effects of biomass reduction are: interception declines, surface retention declines, surface roughness declines, runoff increases, and erosion increases. The strongest hydrologic and erosion responses tend to occur when biomass loss is combined with steep slopes and/or high bare-ground cover, which together create the conditions for concentrated flow and rapid transport of sediment [N2-R2][N2-F1][N4-F3].
node_outputs.N7:
Branch on hydrophobicity’s direct effects on post-fire hydrology

Hydrophobicity after wildfires is a major driver of increased surface runoff because it reduces infiltration. The evidence directly states that fire-induced soil hydrophobicity can inhibit infiltration and produce fire-flood-type debris flows [N1-R1]. Another source says fire-altered soil water repellency influenced infiltration capacity and increased runoff rates immediately after the fire [N1-R2]. A third source explicitly lists “increase in soil water repellency can decrease infiltration and increase surface runoff” as one of the post-fire effects [N1-R3]. These findings align with the broader conceptual framework that hydrophobic soils are less able to absorb water, so more water becomes surface runoff rather than infiltrating into the soil [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

Hydrophobicity also influences soil erosion rates and flow path development. The evidence notes that fire-altered soil water repellency increases runoff rates immediately after the fire and that loss of protective litter decreases surface roughness and increases runoff [N1-R2][N1-R3]. This means hydrophobic soils are not only more prone to rapid surface runoff but also more prone to creating highly concentrated flow paths. The USDA report similarly states that increased post-fire runoff generally facilitates formation of highly erosive concentrated flow and increased soil erosion on hillslopes [N4-F3]. Because hydrophobic soils retain the water-repellent condition, they can sustain lower infiltration even under repeated rainfall events, allowing overland flow to persist and to become more concentrated over time [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F3].

Post-fire conditions that amplify hydrophobicity effects include steep slopes, high rainfall intensity, and coarse-textured soils. The evidence shows that runoff and erosion responses are likely enhanced on steep slopes and under high rainfall intensity [N4-F3]. Coarse-textured soils are especially prone to water repellency, and the literature synthesis states that fire-induced increases in runoff and soil loss are typically greater from areas underneath shrubs and trees than interspaces between canopies [N4-F3]. This matters because steep slopes and high rainfall intensity both increase the volume and energy of overland flow, while coarse-textured soils and canopy cover differences influence how runoff is distributed and how erosion is initiated [N4-F3]. Conversely, hydrophobicity effects are mitigated when infiltration can occur, when vegetation and litter restore surface retention, or when surface roughness is maintained [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F3].

In short, hydrophobicity after wildfire reduces infiltration, increases surface runoff, and promotes erosion by facilitating concentrated flow. Its effects are amplified under steep slopes, high rainfall intensity, and coarse-textured soils, and are mitigated when infiltration or surface retention is preserved [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F3].

Branch on fire severity and burn severity as threshold drivers

The evidence indicates that burn severity is a threshold variable, with different severity classes producing different runoff and erosion responses. The meta-analysis review states that there is a significant effect of fire in runoff and erosion ratios, but different burn severity does not evidence significant differences in post-fire runoff [N3-R1]. This is important because it suggests that, while fire has a broad hydrologic effect, burn severity alone may not always be the strongest predictor of runoff in all studies. In contrast, the same review says amplified runoff and erosion responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N3-R2]. This implies that severity interacts with other site-specific conditions: bare-ground cover and slope are threshold conditions that can trigger stronger post-fire responses than burn severity alone [N3-R2][N3-R1].

Burn severity interacts with biomass loss and hydrophobicity in a coherent way. The meta-analysis review explains that fire-enhanced runoff and erosion are commonly attributed to the partial or total removal of protective soil cover by vegetation and litter, combined with heating-induced changes in soil properties such as aggregate stability and water repellency [N3-F2]. Another source states that high soil burn severity is often associated with a decrease in ground cover, an increase in soil water repellency, and a decrease in infiltration [N3-F2]. Together, these sources show that severe burn conditions are not just about more heat; they also correspond to more biomass loss and more hydrophobic soil, both of which enhance runoff and erosion. This interaction is why burn severity is often used as an indicator of hydrologic and erosion response, even though burn-severity classifications can vary across studies and may not be directly comparable [N3-F2].

Study design and site characteristics strongly affect observed severity responses. The evidence notes that field rainfall simulation experiments (RSEs) have been widely used to study the effects of fire on runoff and erosion, but the most comprehensive recent reviews have not included these RSE studies [N3-F2]. It also says that differences in runoff and erosion between burnt and unburnt RSE plots can be explained by four factors: soil burn severity, time-since-fire, simulated rainfall intensity, and bare soil cover [N3-F2]. This means that observed severity responses depend not just on burn severity itself, but on the rainfall regime, the age of the burn, and the spatial heterogeneity of bare ground. The USDA report similarly emphasizes that runoff and erosion responses are likely enhanced on steep slopes and under high rainfall intensity [N4-F3]. Therefore, severity responses are highly context-dependent; the same burn severity class may produce very different runoff and erosion outcomes across sites with different slopes, rainfall intensity, and post-fire vegetation recovery [N3-F2][N4-F3].

In conclusion, severity classes that produce the strongest runoff and erosion responses are those where biomass loss is large, hydrophobicity is high, and other threshold conditions such as steep slopes and high rainfall intensity are present [N3-R2][N3-F2][N4-F3]. Burn severity interacts with biomass loss and hydrophobicity to create a compound hydrologic effect, while study design and site characteristics such as slope, rainfall intensity, and time-since-fire strongly affect how severity is observed and interpreted [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Branch on thresholds and management implications

The soil and hydrologic thresholds that trigger rapid erosion after wildfire are best understood as combinations of bare ground cover, slope, infiltration capacity, and post-fire vegetation recovery. The evidence states that amplified runoff and erosion responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N4-F3]. It also notes that soil erosion rates are strongly controlled by intrinsic properties such as topography, weather, climate, soil, and vegetation [N4-R4]. In other words, rapid erosion is not triggered by a single threshold but by a set of interacting conditions: when bare ground becomes substantial, when slope becomes steep, and when infiltration is reduced or hydrophobicity persists [N4-F3][N4-R4].

A second threshold is time-since-fire. The evidence indicates that hydrologic and erosion recovery vary with precipitation and ground cover in the years following burning [N4-F3]. This implies that early post-fire conditions are more erosive because vegetation has not yet reestablished, while later recovery may reduce the magnitude of the response. The same source also notes that post-fire runoff and erosion responses are likely enhanced on steep slopes and under high rainfall intensity [N4-F3], which means that rainfall timing and magnitude are important thresholds that can amplify erosion even after initial burn effects have begun to wane [N4-F3].

Management practices that reduce runoff and erosion after wildfires should therefore target both immediate and longer-term recovery. The literature synthesis explicitly states that mitigation treatments are effective when they increase surface cover, trap sediment, and persist through rainfall events [N4-F3]. This points to practices such as mulching, seeding, hydroseeding, and erosion-control structures as ways to restore surface retention and reduce overland flow [N4-F3]. The evidence also supports the use of post-fire stabilization treatments that interact with vegetation and persist through rainfall events, which is especially important because the effectiveness of treatments depends on rainfall intensity and duration [N4-F3].

Model outputs can inform monitoring and mitigation by providing spatially explicit comparisons of runoff and erosion across sites with varied conditions. The evidence notes that the Rangeland Hydrology and Erosion Model (RHEM) provides simultaneous comparisons across multiple sites with varied conditions [N5-R3]. A recent observation-driven modeling framework also considers fire-induced changes to leaf area index and soil saturation, and its hydrologic states include runoff and evapotranspiration [N5-R4]. These models are useful because they can represent the combined effects of biomass loss, hydrophobicity, slope, and rainfall, and they can help identify which areas are most vulnerable to erosion immediately after fire [N5-R3][N5-R4].

The upstream severity branch reinforces these implications by showing that burn severity interacts with biomass loss and hydrophobicity to create compound hydrologic effects [N3-F2]. It also shows that study design and site characteristics affect observed severity responses, meaning that models and monitoring need to account for slope, rainfall intensity, time-since-fire, and bare-ground cover [N3-F2][N4-F3]. In practical terms, this means management should combine post-fire assessment with site-specific modeling, because the same burn severity class can produce very different runoff and erosion outcomes depending on local conditions [N3-F2][N4-F3].

In summary, rapid erosion after wildfire is triggered by thresholds such as 50 to 60 percent bare ground on slopes exceeding 15 percent, high rainfall intensity, and low infiltration or hydrophobicity [N4-F3][N4-R4]. Effective management includes increasing surface cover, trapping sediment, and using persistent treatments that respond to rainfall intensity [N4-F3]. Model outputs can inform monitoring and mitigation by comparing runoff and erosion across sites and by representing the combined effects of burn severity, biomass loss, and slope [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The evidence also suggests that severity responses are highly context-dependent, so monitoring and treatment should be tailored to local site conditions [N3-F2][N4-F3].

# How hydrophobicity and the reduction of aboveground biomass each affect runoff and soil erosion following wildfires

Wildfires change hydrology and erosion in two major ways: **hydrophobicity** and **reduction of aboveground biomass**. Both mechanisms act through distinct but overlapping pathways, and together they create the conditions for increased runoff and soil erosion after fire. The evidence across the branch reports shows that these effects are not isolated; they interact with slope, vegetation structure, burn severity, and site-specific conditions to determine whether the landscape becomes more or less vulnerable to erosion.

---

## 1) Hydrophobicity: a direct driver of reduced infiltration and increased surface runoff

Hydrophobicity after wildfire is one of the strongest direct hydrologic effects. The evidence shows that fire-induced soil hydrophobicity inhibits infiltration and produces fire-flood-type debris flows [N1-R1]. It also says fire-altered soil water repellency influences infiltration capacity and increases runoff rates immediately after the fire [N1-R2]. A separate source explicitly states that “increase in soil water repellency can decrease infiltration and increase surface runoff” [N1-R3].

These findings support a simple but powerful conclusion: **hydrophobic soils do not absorb water well, so more water becomes surface runoff**. In post-fire conditions, this means less water infiltrates into the soil and more water flows over the surface, increasing the potential for erosion.

Hydrophobicity also affects **soil erosion rates and flow path development**. The evidence notes that fire-altered soil water repellency increases runoff rates immediately after the fire, and that loss of protective litter decreases surface roughness and increases runoff [N1-R2][N1-R3]. This means hydrophobic soils are not only more prone to rapid runoff, but also to creating **highly concentrated flow paths** that can entrain and transport more sediment. The broader literature synthesis also states that increased post-fire runoff generally facilitates formation of highly erosive concentrated flow and increased soil erosion on hillslopes [N4-F3].

### Post-fire conditions that amplify or mitigate hydrophobicity effects

The evidence indicates that hydrophobicity effects are amplified under **steep slopes, high rainfall intensity, and coarse-textured soils** [N4-F3]. These conditions increase the volume and energy of overland flow, making hydrophobic soils even more erosive. Coarse-textured soils are especially prone to water repellency, and the literature synthesis says fire-induced increases in runoff and soil loss are typically greater from areas underneath shrubs and trees than interspaces between canopies [N4-F3].

Conversely, hydrophobicity effects are mitigated when infiltration can occur, when vegetation and litter restore surface retention, or when surface roughness is maintained [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F3]. In other words, the hydrologic recovery of the landscape is a key factor in how long hydrophobicity remains a dominant driver of erosion.

---

## 2) Reduction of aboveground biomass: loss of interception, surface retention, and roughness

Aboveground biomass reduction after wildfires primarily alters hydrology by removing the vegetation and litter that control interception and surface retention. The evidence states that fire removal of plants and litter reduces rainfall interception and surface water storage, promoting rapid runoff and decreasing ground-surface protection against raindrop impact and soil detachment [N2-R2]. Another source similarly notes that reductions in ground cover abate surface retention of overland flow, allowing flow to concentrate and move downslope with greater erosive potential [N2-F1].

This is the core mechanism of biomass loss: the vegetation layer that would otherwise intercept some rainfall and store water on the surface is gone. Without it, more water becomes direct runoff rather than being absorbed, retained, or slowed by vegetation [N2-R2][N2-F1].

Reduced surface roughness is another direct consequence of aboveground biomass loss. The same literature synthesis notes that reduced ground cover abates surface retention and allows overland flow to concentrate downslope [N2-F1]. This matters because surface roughness is a key factor in distributing runoff across a hillslope; when it is reduced, flow paths become more concentrated, flow velocity increases, and erosion potential rises [N2-R3][N2-F1].

### How biomass reduction interacts with slope and vegetation structure

The interaction with slope and vegetation structure is important because the effects of biomass reduction are amplified where slopes are steep. The USDA report explicitly says amplified runoff and erosion responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N4-F3]. In other words, biomass reduction interacts with topography: on gentle slopes, some surface retention and dispersion may still occur, but on steep slopes, even a moderate loss of cover can rapidly create conditions favorable to concentrated flow and high erosion rates [N4-F3]. This is consistent with the general idea that vegetation structure and slope together determine how rainfall is partitioned into infiltration, interception, and direct runoff [N2-F1][N4-F3].

---

## 3) Fire severity and burn severity as threshold drivers

Fire severity and burn severity are not just general descriptors of wildfire; they are **threshold drivers** that can determine the magnitude of post-fire runoff and erosion. The evidence indicates that burn severity is a threshold variable, with different severity classes producing different runoff and erosion responses [N3-R1]. However, the same review also says different burn severity does not evidence significant differences in post-fire runoff in all studies [N3-R1], showing that severity is not always the strongest predictor.

The strongest responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N3-R2]. This means burn severity interacts with other site-specific conditions: bare-ground cover and slope are threshold conditions that can trigger stronger post-fire responses than burn severity alone [N3-R2][N3-R1].

The evidence also shows that study design and site characteristics strongly affect observed severity responses. ## 4) Thresholds and management implications

The soil and hydrologic thresholds that trigger rapid erosion after wildfire are best understood as combinations of bare ground cover, slope, infiltration capacity, and post-fire vegetation recovery. The evidence states that amplified runoff and erosion responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N4-F3]. ## Bottom line

After wildfires, **hydrophobicity** and **biomass reduction** both raise runoff and erosion risk, but through different mechanisms. Hydrophobicity weakens infiltration and creates highly erosive flow paths, while biomass reduction removes vegetation and litter that control interception and surface retention [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-F1]. Together, these effects are amplified on steep slopes, under high rainfall intensity, and when bare-ground cover becomes substantial [N4-F3][N3-R2]. The strongest responses are not always tied to a single burn severity class; they depend on a combination of severity, slope, rainfall, and recovery conditions [N3-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence notes that fire-altered soil water repellency increases runoff rates immediately after the fire, and that loss of protective litter decreases surface roughness and increases runoff [N1-R2][N1-R3]. This means hydrophobic soils are not only more prone to rapid runoff, but also to creating **highly concentrated flow paths** that can entrain and transport more sediment. ## 2) Reduction of aboveground biomass: loss of interception, surface retention, and roughness

The evidence states that fire removal of plants and litter reduces rainfall interception and surface water storage, promoting rapid runoff and decreasing ground-surface protection against raindrop impact and soil detachment [N2-R2]. Another source similarly notes that reductions in ground cover abate surface retention of overland flow, allowing flow to concentrate and move downslope with greater erosive potential [N2-F1].

This is the core mechanism of biomass loss: the vegetation layer that would otherwise intercept some rainfall and store water on the surface is gone. Without it, more water becomes direct runoff rather than being absorbed, retained, or slowed by vegetation [N2-R2][N2-F1].

Reduced surface roughness is another direct consequence of aboveground biomass loss. The same literature synthesis notes that reduced ground cover abates surface retention and allows overland flow to concentrate downslope [N2-F1]. This matters because surface roughness is a key factor in distributing runoff across a hillslope; when it is reduced, flow paths become more concentrated, flow velocity increases, and erosion potential rises [N2-R3][N2-F1].

The interaction with slope and vegetation structure is important because the effects of biomass reduction are amplified where slopes are steep. The USDA report explicitly says amplified runoff and erosion responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N4-F3]. In other words, biomass reduction interacts with topography: on gentle slopes, some surface retention and dispersion may still occur, but on steep slopes, even a moderate loss of cover can rapidly create conditions favorable to concentrated flow and high erosion rates [N4-F3]. This is consistent with the general idea that vegetation structure and slope together determine how rainfall is partitioned into infiltration, interception, and direct runoff [N2-F1][N4-F3].

## 3) Fire severity and burn severity as threshold drivers

The evidence also shows that study design and site characteristics strongly affect observed severity responses. ## 4) Thresholds and management implications

The soil and hydrologic thresholds that trigger rapid erosion after wildfire are best understood as combinations of bare ground cover, slope, infiltration capacity, and post-fire vegetation recovery. It also notes that soil erosion rates are strongly controlled by intrinsic properties such as topography, weather, climate, soil, and vegetation [N4-R4]. In other words, rapid erosion is not triggered by a single threshold but by a set of interacting conditions: when bare ground becomes substantial, when slope becomes steep, and when infiltration is reduced or hydrophobicity persists [N4-F3][N4-R4].

A second threshold is **time-since-fire**. The evidence indicates that hydrologic and erosion recovery vary with precipitation and ground cover in the years following burning [N4-F3]. This implies that early post-fire conditions are more erosive because vegetation has not yet reestablished, while later recovery may reduce the magnitude of the response. Management practices that reduce runoff and erosion should target both immediate and longer-term recovery. The literature synthesis explicitly states that mitigation treatments are effective when they increase surface cover, trap sediment, and persist through rainfall events [N4-F3]. This points to practices such as mulching, seeding, hydroseeding, and erosion-control structures as ways to restore surface retention and reduce overland flow [N4-F3]. The evidence also supports the use of post-fire stabilization treatments that interact with vegetation and persist through rainfall events, which is especially important because the effectiveness of treatments depends on rainfall intensity and duration [N4-F3].

## 5) Synthesis: how hydrophobicity and biomass reduction each contribute

After wildfires, **hydrophobicity** and **biomass reduction** both raise runoff and erosion risk, but through different mechanisms. The strongest responses are not always tied to a single burn severity class; they depend on a combination of severity, slope, rainfall, and recovery conditions [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Management should therefore be site-specific, using practices that restore cover and models that can compare runoff and erosion across conditions [N4-F3][N5-R3][N5-R4].

# How hydrophobicity and the reduction of aboveground biomass each affect runoff and soil erosion following wildfires

Wildfires change hydrology and erosion in two major ways: **hydrophobicity** and **reduction of aboveground biomass**. Both mechanisms act through distinct but overlapping pathways, and together they create the conditions for increased runoff and soil erosion after fire. The evidence across the branch reports shows that these effects are not isolated; they interact with slope, vegetation structure, burn severity, and site-specific conditions to determine whether the landscape becomes more or less vulnerable to erosion.

---

Hydrophobicity after wildfire is one of the strongest direct hydrologic effects. A separate source explicitly states that “increase in soil water repellency can decrease infiltration and increase surface runoff” [N1-R3].

These findings support a simple but powerful conclusion: **hydrophobic soils do not absorb water well, so more water becomes surface runoff**. In post-fire conditions, this means less water infiltrates into the soil and more water flows over the surface, increasing the potential for erosion.

Hydrophobicity also affects **soil erosion rates and flow path development**. The evidence notes that fire-altered soil water repellency increases runoff rates immediately after the fire, and that loss of protective litter decreases surface roughness and increases runoff [N1-R2][N1-R3]. This means hydrophobic soils are not only more prone to rapid runoff, but also to creating **highly concentrated flow paths** that can entrain and transport more sediment. The broader literature synthesis also states that increased post-fire runoff generally facilitates formation of highly erosive concentrated flow and increased soil erosion on hillslopes [N4-F3].

### Post-fire conditions that amplify or mitigate hydrophobicity effects

The evidence indicates that hydrophobicity effects are amplified under **steep slopes, high rainfall intensity, and coarse-textured soils** [N4-F3]. These conditions increase the volume and energy of overland flow, making hydrophobic soils even more erosive. Coarse-textured soils are especially prone to water repellency, and the literature synthesis says fire-induced increases in runoff and soil loss are typically greater from areas underneath shrubs and trees than interspaces between canopies [N4-F3].

Conversely, hydrophobicity effects are mitigated when infiltration can occur, when vegetation and litter restore surface retention, or when surface roughness is maintained [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F3]. In other words, the hydrologic recovery of the landscape is a key factor in how long hydrophobicity remains a dominant driver of erosion.

Aboveground biomass reduction after wildfires primarily alters hydrology by removing the vegetation and litter that control interception and surface retention. This is the core mechanism of biomass loss: the vegetation layer that would otherwise intercept some rainfall and store water on the surface is gone. Without it, more water becomes direct runoff rather than being absorbed, retained, or slowed by vegetation [N2-R2][N2-F1].

Reduced surface roughness is another direct consequence of aboveground biomass loss. The same literature synthesis notes that reduced ground cover abates surface retention and allows overland flow to concentrate downslope [N2-F1]. This matters because surface roughness is a key factor in distributing runoff across a hillslope; when it is reduced, flow paths become more concentrated, flow velocity increases, and erosion potential rises [N2-R3][N2-F1].

Management practices that reduce runoff and erosion should target both immediate and longer-term recovery. The literature synthesis explicitly states that mitigation treatments are effective when they increase surface cover, trap sediment, and persist through rainfall events [N4-F3]. - **Hydrophobicity** reduces infiltration and increases surface runoff, while also promoting concentrated flow and higher erosion potential [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F3].

### How biomass reduction interacts with slope and vegetation structure

The interaction with slope and vegetation structure is important because the effects of biomass reduction are amplified where slopes are steep. The USDA report explicitly says amplified runoff and erosion responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N4-F3]. In other words, biomass reduction interacts with topography: on gentle slopes, some surface retention and dispersion may still occur, but on steep slopes, even a moderate loss of cover can rapidly create conditions favorable to concentrated flow and high erosion rates [N4-F3]. This is consistent with the general idea that vegetation structure and slope together determine how rainfall is partitioned into infiltration, interception, and direct runoff [N2-F1][N4-F3].

---

## 3) Fire severity and burn severity as threshold drivers

Fire severity and burn severity are not just general descriptors of wildfire; they are **threshold drivers** that can determine the magnitude of post-fire runoff and erosion. The evidence indicates that burn severity is a threshold variable, with different severity classes producing different runoff and erosion responses [N3-R1]. However, the same review also says different burn severity does not evidence significant differences in post-fire runoff in all studies [N3-R1], showing that severity is not always the strongest predictor.

The strongest responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N3-R2]. This means burn severity interacts with other site-specific conditions: bare-ground cover and slope are threshold conditions that can trigger stronger post-fire responses than burn severity alone [N3-R2][N3-R1].

### How burn severity interacts with biomass loss and hydrophobicity

Burn severity interacts with biomass loss and hydrophobicity in a coherent way. The meta-analysis review explains that fire-enhanced runoff and erosion are commonly attributed to the partial or total removal of protective soil cover by vegetation and litter, combined with heating-induced changes in soil properties such as aggregate stability and water repellency [N3-F2]. Another source states that high soil burn severity is often associated with a decrease in ground cover, an increase in soil water repellency, and a decrease in infiltration [N3-F2]. Together, these sources show that severe burn conditions are not just about more heat; they also correspond to more biomass loss and more hydrophobic soil, both of which enhance runoff and erosion [N3-F2].

### How study design and site characteristics affect observed severity responses

The evidence also shows that study design and site characteristics strongly affect observed severity responses. The evidence notes that field rainfall simulation experiments (RSEs) have been widely used to study the effects of fire on runoff and erosion, but the most comprehensive recent reviews have not included these RSE studies [N3-F2]. It also says that differences in runoff and erosion between burnt and unburnt RSE plots can be explained by four factors: soil burn severity, time-since-fire, simulated rainfall intensity, and bare soil cover [N3-F2]. This means observed severity responses depend not just on burn severity itself, but on the rainfall regime, the age of the burn, and the spatial heterogeneity of bare ground [N3-F2].

The upstream severity branch also emphasizes that runoff and erosion responses are likely enhanced on steep slopes and under high rainfall intensity [N4-F3]. Therefore, severity responses are highly context-dependent; the same burn severity class may produce very different runoff and erosion outcomes across sites with different slopes, rainfall intensity, and post-fire vegetation recovery [N3-F2][N4-F3].

---

## 4) Thresholds and management implications

The soil and hydrologic thresholds that trigger rapid erosion after wildfire are best understood as combinations of bare ground cover, slope, infiltration capacity, and post-fire vegetation recovery. The evidence states that amplified runoff and erosion responses are most likely where fire increases bare ground to 50 to 60 percent and slopes exceed 15 percent [N4-F3]. It also notes that soil erosion rates are strongly controlled by intrinsic properties such as topography, weather, climate, soil, and vegetation [N4-R4]. In other words, rapid erosion is not triggered by a single threshold but by a set of interacting conditions: when bare ground becomes substantial, when slope becomes steep, and when infiltration is reduced or hydrophobicity persists [N4-F3][N4-R4].

A second threshold is **time-since-fire**. The evidence indicates that hydrologic and erosion recovery vary with precipitation and ground cover in the years following burning [N4-F3]. This implies that early post-fire conditions are more erosive because vegetation has not yet reestablished, while later recovery may reduce the magnitude of the response. The same source also notes that post-fire runoff and erosion responses are likely enhanced on steep slopes and under high rainfall intensity [N4-F3], which means that rainfall timing and magnitude are important thresholds that can amplify erosion even after initial burn effects have begun to wane [N4-F3].

### Management practices that reduce runoff and erosion after wildfires

Management practices that reduce runoff and erosion should target both immediate and longer-term recovery. The literature synthesis explicitly states that mitigation treatments are effective when they increase surface cover, trap sediment, and persist through rainfall events [N4-F3]. This points to practices such as mulching, seeding, hydroseeding, and erosion-control structures as ways to restore surface retention and reduce overland flow [N4-F3]. The evidence also supports the use of post-fire stabilization treatments that interact with vegetation and persist through rainfall events, which is especially important because the effectiveness of treatments depends on rainfall intensity and duration [N4-F3].

### How model outputs can inform monitoring and mitigation

Model outputs can inform monitoring and mitigation by providing spatially explicit comparisons of runoff and erosion across sites with varied conditions. The evidence notes that the Rangeland Hydrology and Erosion Model (RHEM) provides simultaneous comparisons across multiple sites with varied conditions [N5-R3]. A recent observation-driven modeling framework also considers fire-induced changes to leaf area index and soil saturation, and its hydrologic states include runoff and evapotranspiration [N5-R4]. These models are useful because they can represent the combined effects of biomass loss, hydrophobicity, slope, and rainfall, and they can help identify which areas are most vulnerable to erosion immediately after fire [N5-R3][N5-R4].

The upstream severity branch reinforces these implications by showing that burn severity interacts with biomass loss and hydrophobicity to create compound hydrologic effects [N3-F2]. It also shows that study design and site characteristics affect observed severity responses, meaning that models and monitoring need to account for slope, rainfall intensity, time-since-fire, and bare-ground cover [N3-F2][N4-F3]. In practical terms, this means management should combine post-fire assessment with site-specific modeling, because the same burn severity class can produce very different runoff and erosion outcomes depending on local conditions [N3-F2][N4-F3].

---

## 5) Synthesis: how hydrophobicity and biomass reduction each contribute

In short, the two mechanisms operate together:

- **Hydrophobicity** reduces infiltration and increases surface runoff, while also promoting concentrated flow and higher erosion potential [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F3].
- **Aboveground biomass reduction** removes interception and surface retention, reduces surface roughness, and increases overland flow and erosion, especially on steep slopes and with high bare-ground cover [N2-R2][N2-F1][N2-R3][N4-F3].
- **Fire severity and burn severity** act as threshold drivers, but their observed effects depend on slope, rainfall intensity, time-since-fire, and other site-specific conditions [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F2][N4-F3].
- **Management** should focus on restoring surface cover, trapping sediment, and using persistent treatments, while models can help identify vulnerable areas and guide monitoring and mitigation [N4-F3][N5-R3][N5-R4].

## Bottom line

After wildfires, **hydrophobicity** and **biomass reduction** both raise runoff and erosion risk, but through different mechanisms. Hydrophobicity weakens infiltration and creates highly erosive flow paths, while biomass reduction removes vegetation and litter that control interception and surface retention [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-F1]. Together, these effects are amplified on steep slopes, under high rainfall intensity, and when bare-ground cover becomes substantial [N4-F3][N3-R2]. The strongest responses are not always tied to a single burn severity class; they depend on a combination of severity, slope, rainfall, and recovery conditions [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Management should therefore be site-specific, using practices that restore cover and models that can compare runoff and erosion across conditions [N4-F3][N5-R3][N5-R4].
